title: Leslie And Ron

jokes.text: I left a rusty hacksaw on the table, so the first person who hacks their face off gets release.
jokes.setup: Ben is explaining the locked-room intervention setup to Leslie and Ron, listing the serious rules
jokes.punchline: He casually adds a rusty hacksaw as a darkly absurd escape option, undercutting the seriousness
jokes.explanation: Good cold-open joke that immediately establishes the absurd stakes of the episode. The specificity of 'rusty hacksaw' and 'hacks their face off' elevates it from generic dark humor. Ben's casual delivery of something horrific is perfectly in character.

dialogue.speaker: Unknown lockdown organizer
dialogue.line: You could always chew your arm off like a trapped animal.

jokes.text: Game of Thrones is on tonight. It's the series finale. Khaleesi is marrying Jack Sparrow. Oh, God, that show has really gone off the rails.
jokes.setup: Ben is protesting being locked in, listing real-world consequences
jokes.punchline: He invents a completely absurd Game of Thrones finale plot (mixing GoT and Pirates of the Caribbean) as if it's real, then critiques the show for being off the rails
jokes.explanation: This is a standout joke. The structure is layered: Ben uses a fake pop culture complaint to seem relatable, the absurdity of the crossover escalates perfectly, and then his deadpan 'that show has really gone off the rails' lands as both self-aware critique and character comedy. The joke works on multiple levels — it's a Parks writers' room joke about TV shows, a character moment showing Ben's nerdy sincerity, and pure absurdist comedy. Comparable in cleverness to the 8.0 anchor.

dialogue.speaker: Ben Wyatt
dialogue.line: We need to find that Game of Thrones finale before anyone spoils it!

dialogue.speaker: April Ludgate
dialogue.line: I heard Captain Jack Sparrow takes the Iron Throne and declares himself King of the Seven Seas.

dialogue.speaker: Ben Wyatt
dialogue.line: What? That's not how Game of Thrones ends.

dialogue.speaker: April Ludgate
dialogue.line: Then Daenerys marries Will Turner and they sail off to find the Fountain of Youth.

jokes.text: It makes sense if you've read the books.
jokes.setup: Ben himself just said the Khaleesi/Jack Sparrow plot means GoT has 'gone off the rails'
jokes.punchline: He immediately defends it with the classic book-reader's excuse, contradicting his own critique
jokes.explanation: Exceptional economy — five words that land perfectly as a callback to the immediately preceding joke. The character integration is near-perfect: only Ben Wyatt, the biggest nerd in the Parks universe, would defend his own absurd invention by citing fictional source material. The self-contradiction is the joke, and it's executed with immaculate brevity. Strong 8 in craft for economy and character specificity alone.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Look, in the books, it's all explained. The showrunners just didn't have time to develop that storyline properly.

jokes.text: I am going to break out of here, then I am going to snap you in half.
jokes.setup: The group is reacting to being locked in; the tone is anxious
jokes.punchline: Ron escalates to direct physical threat with complete calm, as if it's a reasonable next step
jokes.explanation: Very Ron Swanson. The flat delivery of violent intent is signature character comedy. The joke is less original than it seems — it's a well-worn Swanson beat — but the specificity of 'snap you in half' and the calm rationality of it saves it from being generic.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Terry, we really need your help on this.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: For once, I agree with her.

dialogue.speaker: Terry
dialogue.line: I don't know, you two are always fighting.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Ron's right, Terry. Just this once, can't you—

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Why are you making this so difficult?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Yeah, Terry!

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: This is ridiculous.

jokes.text: This is not his fault, Swanson. Be a man, and get your house in order. You too, Knope.
jokes.setup: Ron has just threatened to snap someone in half; April is supposed to be empathetic
jokes.punchline: April delivers a tough-love speech that is completely unsentimental and borderline harsh, undercutting the emotional moment
jokes.explanation: April's blunt, anti-sentimental voice is well-deployed here. It's a minor laugh — the joke is that she's supposed to comfort them but instead delivers a gruff command. Functional character comedy.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: You're going to hurt yourself.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I would prefer that to having a conversation about my feelings.

jokes.text: Terry, look at me. Is this what you want to do? Think very carefully, son.
jokes.setup: Terry is hesitating between following Ben/April's plan and heeding Ron's warning
jokes.punchline: Ron addresses Terry with paternal gravitas as if this is a life-or-death moral crossroads, weaponizing the fact that Terry always crumbles under authority
jokes.explanation: The joke is Ron's paternal condescension toward Terry ('son') combined with treating the locking-in as a moral test. It works because it's character-specific: Ron's gravitas is always disproportionate, and Terry's spinelessness is a running gag.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: We'll say we broke up because I cared too much. I was too invested in the relationship, too passionate, too committed to making it work.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: That's not a flaw, Leslie.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I know. That's why it's perfect.

jokes.text: Both: Damn it, Terry! [triumphant music]
jokes.setup: Terry defies Ron's warning and follows the plan; Ron and Leslie both react
jokes.punchline: Despite being on opposite sides of the conflict, Ron and Leslie unite in their exasperation at Terry, accompanied by triumphant music — which is for Ben/April's plan succeeding, not for Terry
jokes.explanation: This is a well-earned running gag payoff with a structural twist: Leslie and Ron are currently enemies, but Terry transcends their feud. The triumphant music scoring Terry's 'betrayal' is a nice ironic visual/audio gag. The moment is economical and character-rich.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Ron would never admit it, but deep down, I think he actually respects me.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: You're a butthead.

jokes.text: I would rather bleed out than sit here and talk about my feelings for ten hours.
jokes.setup: Leslie warns Ron that punching through the security-wired window will slice his arm open
jokes.punchline: Ron calmly states he prefers bleeding to death over emotional conversation
jokes.explanation: High character integration — this is the platonic ideal of a Ron Swanson joke. His anti-feelings philosophy taken to its logical extreme (preferring death). 'Bleed out' is perfectly specific and 'ten hours' grounds the absurdity. Highly quotable. Loses points on originality since the 'Ron hates feelings' well is well-established, but the execution here is clean.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Why do I have to be the problem?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Because you're being reasonable, Ron. That's like a science fiction scenario.

jokes.text: I'll just tell them that I apologized for... whatever, heroically caring too much, and you admitted that you're a stubborn butthead.
jokes.setup: Leslie is proposing they lie to Ben about having resolved things
jokes.punchline: Her version of 'her fault' is 'heroically caring too much' — she can't even pretend to be in the wrong without making herself the hero
jokes.explanation: Excellent character comedy. Leslie's inability to cast herself as the villain even in a hypothetical lie is deeply true to who she is. 'Heroically caring too much' is the perfect self-mythologizing phrase. Strong character integration score — this could only be Leslie.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I will not be blamed for this.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: No, no, Ron. This is on me. I take full responsibility. I'm the one who made the decision, and I'm the one who has to live with the consequences. But you know what? That's what leadership is. It's about standing up and saying 'I did this,' even when it's hard. Even when everyone's going to hate you for it. I'm just glad I have the strength and the moral clarity to do what needs to be done, unlike some people who only think about themselves.

jokes.text: Why do I have to be stubborn? Why can't the problem have been that I was reasonable?
jokes.setup: Leslie assigns Ron the role of 'stubborn butthead' in their fake reconciliation narrative
jokes.punchline: Ron objects — not to being called a problem, but to the characterization. His proposed alternative ('I was reasonable') is played completely straight
jokes.explanation: A nice reversal — Ron's pride is so specific that he'd rather be called a 'reasonable problem' than a stubborn one. The joke works because of Ron's refusal to participate in any narrative he doesn't control.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I respect that.

jokes.text: Because we want them to believe us and not laugh really hard at a ridiculous science fiction scenario.
jokes.setup: Ron asks why he can't be 'the reasonable one' in their fake story
jokes.punchline: Leslie explains that Ron being reasonable is so implausible it falls into science fiction
jokes.explanation: Competent comeback. The 'science fiction' framing is a nice escalation of the insult but it's not especially surprising or fresh. Functional.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Ron, what are you doing?

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I'm destroying this phone. It's the only way to be sure.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Ron, no! That's our only—

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I don't care.

jokes.text: Fine! I'll tell them that for the past three years, you've been a perfect gentleman and scholar, and I am an insane weirdo who, despite being the only reason we even had a friendship to begin with, decided to ruin it out of the blue for no good reason.
jokes.setup: The negotiation over their fake story has broken down
jokes.punchline: Leslie's 'Fine, I'll take all the blame' speech is so hilariously self-aware and laced with passive-aggressive qualifiers that it becomes its own argument
jokes.explanation: This is a great Leslie Knope joke. She's ostensibly conceding but every clause of her 'concession' is a self-serving rewrite. 'Despite being the only reason we even had a friendship to begin with' is the gem — it's buried in a sentence that's nominally self-deprecating but is actually self-aggrandizing. The structure mirrors Leslie's psychology perfectly. Strong 8 for impact because the escalation lands well.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Ron, you just locked yourself out of your own office.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I'm aware.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: With the keys still inside.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Yes, Leslie, I can see them from here.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: So what's your plan?

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I didn't think that far ahead.

jokes.text: That sounds good. Let's go with that.
jokes.setup: Leslie delivers a scorching fake-concession speech
jokes.punchline: Ron's response is completely flat and agreeable — he heard her agree to take the blame and that's all he needed
jokes.explanation: Perfect economy — five words that hilariously miss the entire point of Leslie's passive-aggressive rant. Ron's flat approval is funnier than any counter-argument could be. The joke is entirely in the underreaction, which is deeply Ron.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I've never learned anyone's name. I'm not interested.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: But Ron, you literally just called me by my name.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: No I didn't, Brenda.

jokes.text: I destroyed the monitor! / What if we have an emergency and have to get out of here? / I did not consider that possibility!
jokes.setup: Leslie turns on the baby monitor to signal Ben; Ron smashes it rather than comply
jokes.punchline: When Leslie points out the obvious flaw in his plan, Ron's response is completely unguarded self-admission with no defensiveness
jokes.explanation: The joke works on two levels: Ron's impulsive, prideful self-destruction is funny, and his complete honesty about the oversight ('I did not consider that possibility!') is funnier. There's no bluster or cover-up — just pure Ron admitting the obvious. The exclamation mark delivery sells it as almost proud self-awareness.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I accept your wager. However, I must insist upon the following terms and conditions: First, all dialogue must be conducted in English, or possibly Latin. Second, any and all utterances I make shall be notarized and filed with the Pawnee Parks Department. Third, should I emerge victorious, you must publicly acknowledge my superiority in matters of discourse. Fourth, I reserve the right to communicate exclusively through interpretive dance should I deem it necessary. Fifth, this agreement is binding in perpetuity and across all known dimensions. Sixth, no talking about feelings. Seventh, that's it. Those are my terms.

jokes.text: I tried not to notice anything when I worked here. Or talk to anyone. Or learn anyone's name. You, of all people, should know that, Lauren.
jokes.setup: Leslie notices the office has been redecorated; Ron comments
jokes.punchline: Ron's escalating list of antisocial behaviors culminates in calling Leslie by the wrong name — undermining his point about knowing people
jokes.explanation: One of the best jokes in the episode. The structure is near-perfect: Ron builds a case for his antisocial philosophy through a list, and then the punchline is embedded in the final address — calling Leslie 'Lauren' proves his point while simultaneously making him look ridiculous. The joke is entirely about character (only Ron would say this), has perfect economy, and the payoff is completely earned. Comparable in construction to an 8.0-anchor-quality joke but with superior character integration. Highly quotable and has strong rewatch value.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Ron, come on, talk to me. Ron? Ron, please? RON? Ron! Ron, Ron, Ron, Ron! Ron? RON! Ron Ron Ron! R-Ron? Ron... Ron. Ron?

jokes.text: I choose 'sit here.' / Come on, Ron, why don't we just-- / Sit here. / Ron. / Sit here.
jokes.setup: Leslie offers to discuss their issues; Ron responds
jokes.punchline: Ron's repeated 'Sit here' as an answer to every escalation is funny through sheer stubborn repetition
jokes.explanation: A functional bit that works through repetition. The comedy is in Ron's total immovability and his refusal to even engage with Leslie's escalating pleas. It's a decent bit but doesn't transcend the formula.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Ron, you love plastic. You're basically a petrochemical lobbyist.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I love wood. I have spent thousands of hours perfecting my craft.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Wood is just plastic that hasn't been processed yet.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: That is the dumbest thing I have ever heard.

jokes.text: I'll take that bet at any odds, for any amount of money, over any length of time stretching from now into infinity.
jokes.setup: Leslie bets she can make Ron talk
jokes.punchline: Ron's response is a legal-style all-encompassing acceptance of the bet, meant to convey absolute confidence in his silence
jokes.explanation: The joke is the grandiosity of Ron's commitment. 'Stretching from now into infinity' is the escalation that makes it work — he turns a simple bet into a declaration of eternal defiance. Very Ron, well-executed.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: My memory is a steel trap of friendship nuggets.

jokes.text: I think wood is stupid, and so does everybody else. You guys, Ron loves plastic.
jokes.setup: Leslie is trying to provoke Ron into speaking by attacking the thing he loves most
jokes.punchline: She makes increasingly ridiculous anti-wood claims, culminating in the absurd 'Ron loves plastic'
jokes.explanation: The joke relies on shared knowledge that Ron's love of wood is sacred. Leslie weaponizing this is smart, and 'Ron loves plastic' is the perfect escalation — the worst possible insult for Ron Swanson. Works well as character comedy.

jokes.text: a fact I remember because my mind is a steel trap of friendship nuggets.
jokes.setup: Leslie announces she remembers which song Ron chose at a 2007 barbecue
jokes.punchline: Her justification — 'steel trap of friendship nuggets' — is a hilariously specific and slightly absurd coinage
jokes.explanation: Steel trap of friendship nuggets' is an exceptional phrase. It captures Leslie's obsessive, categorized warmth in a single image. 'Steel trap' is a cliché repurposed brilliantly by pairing it with 'friendship nuggets' — a Leslie-specific coinage that feels entirely authentic. Highly quotable and earns its 8.0 craft score through originality and character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: 🎵 Don't stop... believing... hold on to that feeeeeling... 🎵

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: 🎵 Streetlight... people... living just to find emotion... 🎵

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: 🎵 And Ben is really tall and he's so smart and handsome... 🎵

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: 🎵 I love waffles more than breakfast foods... I really do... 🎵

jokes.text: I'm gonna play Jerry's choice. [Billy Joel's We Didn't Start the Fire plays] Ooh, that's right. And I'm gonna maintain eye contact the whole time.
jokes.setup: Leslie is using music as psychological torture; she announces she'll play the most annoying choice — Jerry's
jokes.punchline: Jerry predictably chose 'We Didn't Start the Fire,' the most characteristically uncool choice possible, and Leslie maintaining eye contact amplifies the cruelty
jokes.explanation: The joke works on multiple levels: it's a running gag about Jerry/Terry's uncoolness, it's a perfect music choice for the character, and Leslie maintaining eye contact is a great visual comedy beat that elevates simple mockery into performance art. The setup and payoff are tight.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: 🎵 You're gonna die alone, in a corner, no one will find you for weeks... Your skin will slough off and bugs will eat your face... 🎵

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: 🎵 Diarrhea, diarrhea, diarrhea, diarrhea, diarrhea, diarrhea, your butt is made of poop! 🎵

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: 🎵 Poop, poop, poop, poop, poop, I'm a toilet, flush me down, chocolate soft serve ice cream swirl! 🎵

jokes.text: ♪ Harry Truman was a guy / ♪ America, Red China / ♪ All the countries, other people / ♪ Everyone is fun / ♪ Joe Mantegna, Ian McKellen / ♪ I have to buy a new toaster / ♪ This is awesome, you're so stupid / ♪ Jumping up and down ♪
jokes.setup: Leslie plays 'We Didn't Start the Fire' and announces she doesn't know the words
jokes.punchline: Her improvised lyrics are brilliantly wrong — mixing real historical names with mundane thoughts, random celebrity names, and direct-to-Ron taunts
jokes.explanation: This is the comedic peak of the episode. The fake We Didn't Start the Fire lyrics are a brilliant piece of writing — they parody the song's structure (lists of names/events) while inserting mundane nonsense ('I have to buy a new toaster'), random celebrities (Joe Mantegna, Ian McKellen), and then a direct taunt ('This is awesome, you're so stupid'). The escalation through 'Daddy ate a squirrel' and 'Peter Piper pee-pee poopy' is gleefully juvenile but earns it. The maintained eye contact makes it a visual gag as well. One of the most quotable moments in the episode. Genuinely exceptional writing.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: You have five minutes.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Five minutes? Ron, I need at least ten to explain my vision for the new community garden initiative.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Four minutes fifty seconds.

jokes.text: ♪ Freddy Krueger bought some pants / ♪ Oprah has a turtle farm / ♪ Peter Piper pee-pee poopy / ♪ Daddy ate a squirrel ♪
jokes.setup: First verse of fake lyrics established the bit; second verse continues it
jokes.punchline: The second verse escalates the absurdity — 'Peter Piper pee-pee poopy' is deliberately childish, and 'Daddy ate a squirrel' is weirdly specific and dark
jokes.explanation: The second verse lands even harder than the first because the escalation is earned. 'Peter Piper pee-pee poopy' is a masterclass in committing to the bit — it's juvenile on purpose and that's what makes it great. 'Daddy ate a squirrel' is inexplicably specific and dark. This verse breaks Ron, which gives it structural payoff too.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: We've been best friends for ten years!

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I've worked in the same office as you for ten years. Our relationship is professional, cordial, and limited to work-related interactions and the occasional public event.

jokes.text: Stop this! / ♪ Eisenhower, vaccine ♪ / I will speak with you for three minutes.
jokes.setup: Leslie has been singing fake lyrics for over a minute; Ron finally breaks
jokes.punchline: Ron's capitulation is not emotional — it's a negotiated surrender with a time limit. 'Three minutes' is the perfect specific number.
jokes.explanation: The payoff to the entire song sequence. Ron's pride won't let him just say 'okay, let's talk' — he has to impose a time limit and frame it as a concession with terms. 'Three minutes' is perfect: specific enough to be funny, short enough to be insulting, formal enough to be very Ron. Leslie continuing the song through his first attempt to speak is also a great beat.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I'm going to save our friendship. I have a weapon.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: A binder. A friendship binder. With sections for memories, inside jokes, and a timeline of our relationship.

jokes.text: [high-pitched beep] — Leslie sets a timer on her phone after Ron agrees to three minutes
jokes.setup: Ron agrees to talk for exactly three minutes
jokes.punchline: Leslie immediately sets a timer — she was prepared for exactly this negotiation
jokes.explanation: A small but effective character beat. The fact that Leslie immediately has a timer ready (inferred from context) suggests she anticipated exactly this scenario. It's a visual gag / reaction beat that reinforces her preparedness without a word of explanation.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I said what I said.

jokes.text: We were work proximity associates.
jokes.setup: Leslie says 'We were friends for ten years'
jokes.punchline: Ron's flat correction with 'work proximity associates' reframes their entire relationship with bureaucratic detachment
jokes.explanation: This is among the best lines in the episode. 'Work proximity associates' is a perfectly constructed coinage — it's bureaucratic, specific, and emotionally devastating as a denial of friendship. It works as both a great joke and a thematic statement about Ron's worldview. The phrase itself is instantly quotable and has become somewhat culturally known. Near-perfect character integration: only Ron Swanson would coin this term, deliver it deadpan, and mean it completely. Economy is flawless — three words do the work of a paragraph.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: April's party theme is 'Steampunk Victorian Ghost Hunters in Space.' She combined four completely unrelated aesthetic movements into one party.

jokes.text: and I will do so using the most powerful tool known to man: a well-organized chart.
jokes.setup: Leslie announces she's going to save their friendship using 'the most powerful tool known to man'
jokes.punchline: The dramatic buildup pays off with 'a well-organized chart' — perfectly Leslie
jokes.explanation: The setup is a deliberate dramatic misdirection — 'most powerful tool known to man' suggests something profound — and the punchline is perfectly calibrated to Leslie's character. Only Leslie Knope would make a chart to save a friendship, and only Leslie would describe it with that level of reverence. Solid 8 on craft.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: The Rexford Thistlebottom Estate

jokes.text: At her request, the party's theme is 'Zombie Teenage Biker Gang Pizza Jamboree.' You made me wear a leather jacket.
jokes.setup: Leslie is narrating a timeline of events, noting that April came to work for her and they threw her a party
jokes.punchline: The party theme is a gleefully specific April Ludgate-branded absurdity, and the detail of Ron being made to wear a leather jacket is the visual punchline
jokes.explanation: The party theme name is excellent April characterization — every element (zombie, teenage, biker gang, pizza, jamboree) is perfectly chosen. The added detail of Ron in a leather jacket is a great visual gag implied through dialogue. Good character comedy for both April and Ron.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Ron, I've been working on this timeline for weeks. Look at all the detail.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Impressive. Very thorough.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Right? So what do you think about phase three?

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: It's perfect. Well, I'd better get going.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Going? We just started. Ron, where are you—

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I made a key to the back door months ago.

jokes.text: [British accent] 'Oh, dear. We live at the Morningstar. That's so posh and hibbley-fibbley-gibbley.'
jokes.setup: Leslie is ranting about Ron naming his building 'Morningstar'
jokes.punchline: She impersonates a posh Morningstar resident with a fake British accent and a made-up word: 'hibbley-fibbley-gibbley'
jokes.explanation: 'Hibbley-fibbley-gibbley' is inspired nonsense. The joke works because Leslie's impersonation of pretentious apartment residents is both specific and slightly unhinged. The made-up word captures her frustration better than any real word could. Good character comedy showing Leslie's anti-pretension and her creative insult vocabulary.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Those aren't violations, Leslie. They're features. The rat droppings add an earthy flavor to the flour. The mold on the walls is natural penicillin. And the fact that we haven't updated our inventory system since 1987 means we're honoring history.

jokes.text: The world needs apartment buildings. The park you built is nice, and people want to live next to it.
jokes.setup: Leslie is furious about Morningstar 'ruining' her park
jokes.punchline: Ron's completely reasonable defense is funny because of its flat, obvious pragmatism delivered against Leslie's emotional storm
jokes.explanation: The comedy here is structural — Ron's calm logic against Leslie's passion. It's more character contrast than joke. Functional but not particularly crafted.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: It's not 'JJ's Diner,' Ron. It's 'J.J.'s Diner.' With periods.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I know.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: You kept calling it 'JJ's Diner' this whole time.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I was aware. It wasn't the reason I didn't go there.

jokes.text: Enjoy your new job, Judas.
jokes.setup: Leslie is in a passionate confrontation with Ron over the Morningstar development
jokes.punchline: She exits by calling him 'Judas' — an absurdly Biblical escalation for a zoning dispute
jokes.explanation: A single word doing a lot of work. 'Judas' is a perfect Leslie Knope exit insult — dramatic, historically overwrought, and entirely sincere. The comedy is in the disproportionality. Economy score is high because one word conveys everything.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I have a land mine in my office. For decoration.

jokes.text: Your metaphors are so beautiful.
jokes.setup: Ron describes his work as 'bleeding the rotting beast from the inside'
jokes.punchline: Leslie's earnest, admiring response to Ron's grotesque metaphor is funny because she means it completely
jokes.explanation: Five words that perfectly encapsulate Leslie's relationship with Ron — she genuinely loves his worldview even when she disagrees with it. The joke is her unironic admiration for something objectively gross. Great character moment in a mostly dramatic stretch.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I have a constitutional right to blow up this door.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Actually, the First Amendment protects free speech, not the right to blow things up.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Well, I'm exercising my right to free speech by saying I'm going to blow up this door.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: That's... that's not how that works.

jokes.text: Is it because I sent you a strongly worded letter through the US mail, so the post office knew your address? / No. Go away.
jokes.setup: Leslie is interrogating Ron about why he left Parks; she's guessing wrong causes
jokes.punchline: The post office detail is absurdly specific — she's implying Ron was upset about having his address known by a government agency
jokes.explanation: The detail about 'so the post office knew your address' is the joke — it assumes Ron's libertarian paranoia about government surveillance. This is good character comedy that requires knowing Ron well. The payoff is that it's wrong, which is fine.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: It's actually a party favor that plays 'For He's a Jolly Good Fellow'

jokes.text: They had fresh produce out right next to the roach spray.
jokes.setup: Leslie asks if Ron is upset because she had Food and Stuff shut down for health code violations
jokes.punchline: Ron unintentionally defends the health code violation by describing it as actually reasonable to be upset about
jokes.explanation: Ron's reflexive defense of a store with poor food safety practices is perfectly in character — his anti-government-regulation libertarianism extends even to things that clearly should be regulated. The specificity of 'fresh produce right next to the roach spray' makes the joke land.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I'm disappointed. I thought it was a real mine.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Ron, it's a fake mine. We built it this morning out of cardboard and creativity.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Well, I was very impressed.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Ron, you thought a cardboard mine was real?

jokes.text: The name of the store is 'Food and Stuff.' They sell food, and they sell stuff. If you don't like it, go to that new place, Complete Food.
jokes.setup: Ron just said the store mixing produce with roach spray made sense to him
jokes.punchline: Leslie doubles down by explaining 'Food and Stuff' with deadpan literalism, then calls Whole Foods 'Complete Food' — a perfect near-miss renaming
jokes.explanation: 'Complete Food' for Whole Foods is a brilliant near-miss — it's exactly wrong in a way that makes you appreciate how specifically correct 'Whole' is. The literalist breakdown of 'Food and Stuff' is also a good bit. Solid wordplay comedy.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Welcome to the Ramsett Park Mine. I'm Leslie Knope, and I'm here to tell you about the rich history of mining in Pawnee. Did you know that miners used to work in the dark? That's why they were called... coal miners. Get it? Coal? Dark? I crack myself up.

jokes.text: It's called Whole Foods.
jokes.setup: Leslie calls Whole Foods 'Complete Food'
jokes.punchline: Ron's flat correction implies he knows exactly what Whole Foods is, which is mildly funny given his anti-establishment worldview
jokes.explanation: A small button on joke #34. The comedy is purely in Ron knowing the correct corporate name despite his libertarian persona. Minor laugh, functional.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Are you mad at me because of the party supplies?

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I'm not mad at you, Leslie. I'm mad at the mine.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: But you seem really upset.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: That's just my face.

jokes.text: As many as I need to to solve this mystery and get us engaged in a deep and stimulating conversation about our friendship.
jokes.setup: Ron asks how many more guesses she'll make
jokes.punchline: Leslie describes their inevitable emotional conversation as a 'deep and stimulating' goal she's pursuing, framing friendship as a problem to be solved with bureaucratic determination
jokes.explanation: Leslie's framing of friendship as a 'mystery to solve' is a nice character beat. The joke is in her relentless systematizing of human connection. Functional but not exceptional.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Ron, Ron! Look at this. This is it. This is the smoking gun. This document proves everything.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: What is that?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: It's a memo from the city manager's office about the zoning variance. It's absolutely crucial.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Leslie, that's a hazardous waste disposal form. You're holding it like it's going to give you radiation poisoning.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: What? No, it's—

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Please step away from me.

jokes.text: Detonator. The partially defused claymore mine you gave me ten years ago. I'm gonna use it to blow a hole in this damn door so I can get out of here.
jokes.setup: Ron is searching through a desk for an escape tool
jokes.punchline: He finds — and plans to use — a claymore mine he apparently keeps casually in his office as a gift from Leslie
jokes.explanation: The revelation that Ron has kept a partially defused claymore mine on his desk for a decade — as a gift — is deeply Ron Swanson. It sets up the subsequent reveal beautifully. The 'partially defused' qualifier is perfect dark comedy detail. Strong character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Ron wrote: 'Leslie Knope is a communist.'

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Well, I'm not a communist. I'm a capitalist. But if Ron thinks I'm a communist, that's basically a compliment coming from him.

jokes.text: I'm being held as a prisoner against my will, and I have the right, as a citizen of the United States, to blow a hole in that door and walk out as a free man. It's in the Constitution.
jokes.setup: Ron is about to detonate a claymore mine inside a building
jokes.punchline: He invokes the Constitution to justify detonating an explosive, with complete sincerity — and the joke is that he's absolutely wrong about what the Constitution says
jokes.explanation: Ron's libertarian worldview extended to its most absurd logical conclusion — using Constitutional rights to justify blowing up a door. 'It's in the Constitution' as a statement of absolute certainty about something that clearly isn't is perfect Ron Swanson. High character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Ron predicts mutual murder while considering hiring

jokes.text: There's no cursing in the Constitution.
jokes.setup: Ron says it's in the Constitution (as Ron detonates with a bleep for a swear word)
jokes.punchline: Leslie's objection is not to the legal claim but to the profanity, treating the profanity as the more notable violation
jokes.explanation: Near-perfect economy — six words that reframe the entire joke. Ron invokes the Constitution for illegal explosives; Leslie's correction is about swearing. The misdirection (we expect pushback on the Constitutional claim; instead we get a grammar/propriety correction) is beautifully executed. The joke reveals Leslie's priorities hilariously. Strong 8 on craft.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Despite everything, I recommended hiring her.

jokes.text: [For He's a Jolly Good Fellow plays from the 'claymore mine' — which explodes into balloons and confetti]
jokes.setup: Ron confidently detonates what he believes is a dangerous claymore mine
jokes.punchline: The mine plays 'For He's a Jolly Good Fellow' and releases balloons and confetti — it was a gift from Leslie all along
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best physical comedy moments. The setup (Ron keeping a claymore mine on his desk for a decade, fully prepared to use it) pays off with the reveal that it was always a Leslie Knope party favor. The song choice ('For He's a Jolly Good Fellow') is perfect — celebratory and absurd. The joke is also a beautiful character moment about their friendship. Structure score is high because the payoff perfectly mirrors the setup without being predictable.

dialogue.speaker: Janitor
dialogue.line: Don't be cruel, to a heart that's true. I ain't too proud to beg, sweet darling, please...

jokes.text: You told me this was a genuine partially defused claymore mine. / Well, it was. I bought the empty shell off of eBay, and then I filled it with, you know, balloons and confetti and such.
jokes.setup: Ron confronts Leslie about the fake claymore
jokes.punchline: Leslie's explanation — eBay shell, filled with balloons — is delivered as if the thought process behind it was completely normal
jokes.explanation: The specific detail of buying the empty shell 'off of eBay' is the joke's backbone — it shows how much premeditation and bizarre dedication went into this gift. 'Balloons and confetti and such' delivered casually by Leslie is perfect. The word 'such' does a lot of comic work. Strong character integration for Leslie.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Jerry! Jerry, wait! I will do anything you want. I will eat cubed cheese instead of sliced. I will watch network television. I will go to an Applebee's.

dialogue.speaker: Jerry
dialogue.line: Why would you say that?

jokes.text: You mean to tell me I have had a toy on my desk for ten years? / You mean to tell me you've thought you had an actual land mine on your desk?
jokes.setup: Ron is outraged at being tricked; Leslie flips the perspective
jokes.punchline: Leslie's counter-question reveals that the situation is equally absurd from both angles — Ron's outrage at the deception is undercut by the absurdity of him having a land mine at work
jokes.explanation: The parallel structure of these two questions is elegant — each exposes the other's absurdity. Ron is outraged about having a toy; Leslie is reasonably incredulous that he thought he had real explosives. The reversal perfectly balances the comedy and earns its 8.0 impact score.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Leslie called me a heartless thug.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: You are a heartless thug, Ron.

jokes.text: [Recording plays] 'Congratulations, Ron. You've been doing an explosive job!'
jokes.setup: The fake claymore mine has just exploded with balloons; the gift reveals itself
jokes.punchline: A recorded message from Leslie plays with a mine/explosion pun: 'explosive job'
jokes.explanation: The pun is groan-worthy in the best way — 'explosive job' from a fake claymore mine is the kind of terrible-but-charming joke that perfectly characterizes Leslie's gifts. It's funny because it's a little bad. The recording playing from the balloon-stuffed shell is a great visual bit.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: It was actually just about the brownies

jokes.text: Come on, Ron. It's funny stuff. Who gets angry at balloons?
jokes.setup: Ron is visibly furious at having been deceived for a decade
jokes.punchline: Leslie's completely unbothered, slightly confused response ('Who gets angry at balloons?') treats Ron's fury as irrational
jokes.explanation: Good button on the sequence. 'Who gets angry at balloons?' is a perfectly Leslie deflection — she treats a reasonable grievance as absurd, and technically she's right that getting mad at balloons is strange. The joke works by making the wronged party seem like the unreasonable one.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Maybe Ron finally snapped because he found out he has some French ancestry and couldn't handle the idea of being even one percent French.

jokes.text: Is that nuclear waste? / No, this is my job application from when you hired me. / How did you get that? / Freedom of Information Act request.
jokes.setup: Leslie produces a document from a mysterious container; Ron assumes the worst
jokes.punchline: She got her own job application via FOIA — which is both characteristically Leslie (using government tools she loves) and slightly absurd (treating her own employment file as a state secret)
jokes.explanation: 'Nuclear waste' as a guess is a great quick gag on Ron's paranoid worldview. The FOIA reveal is very Leslie — she used the most formal bureaucratic process available to obtain a personal document. The juxtaposition works well. Good character comedy.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I'm not sure why I pulled the fire alarm. I was just trying to get everyone's attention.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Ron, you're soaking wet and wearing... are those yoga pants?

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I was at hot yoga. It's the worst hour of my life.

jokes.text: This is the Rosetta Stone, Ron. The beginning of the whole shebang.
jokes.setup: Leslie explains the significance of her job application
jokes.punchline: She calls a bureaucratic employment form 'the Rosetta Stone' — an absurdly grand comparison that only Leslie would make earnestly
jokes.explanation: Leslie's tendency to mythologize bureaucratic documents is well-deployed here. It's a mild joke — the comedy is in the disproportionate reverence — but it sets up the application reveal well.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I'm not sure what I'm doing here. I don't believe in yoga. It's a lot of standing around pretending to be a tree. But I'll admit, I do feel... calm.

jokes.text: Why would anyone need more than three lines? I'm describing a person, not something complicated like a wooden sailing ship or proper dovetail technique.
jokes.setup: Leslie is shocked that Ron's hiring recommendation was only three lines
jokes.punchline: Ron's hierarchy of complexity — people are simple, wooden sailing ships and dovetail joints are complicated — is a perfect inversion of normal values, entirely specific to Ron
jokes.explanation: This is one of the best jokes in the episode. The inversion — people are simple; woodworking is the complicated thing — is a perfect crystallization of Ron Swanson's philosophy. 'Dovetail technique' is the specifically perfect woodworking detail (not just 'carpentry' or 'woodworking' — the specific joint). The joke is original, character-essential, and beautifully economical. High marks across all dimensions. Comparable to the 8.0 anchor in craft but with better character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Ron, stop complaining about your appearance. You've survived worse. You got trapped in that pit for three days. You were attacked by a swarm of bees. You accidentally drank paint thinner. A little wrinkle is nothing.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Those were character-building experiences.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Exactly. So this wrinkle is just adding to your character.

jokes.text: I forgot what I wrote. Can I hear it?
jokes.setup: Ron wrote the application three lines long and insists it was sufficient
jokes.punchline: He immediately admits he doesn't remember what those three lines said — undercutting his own confidence
jokes.explanation: A small but effective beat. Ron's bravado about the three-line assessment deflates instantly with his admission that he forgot what he wrote. The childlike 'Can I hear it?' is disarmingly sweet. Economy is high — the turnaround is abrupt and perfectly timed.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Terry is the best at being completely mindless.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I agree.

jokes.text: 'Leslie Knope is an absurd idealist and is slightly to the left of Leon Trotsky.' So far, so accurate.
jokes.setup: Leslie reads Ron's three-line assessment of her from her 2009 job application
jokes.punchline: Ron immediately endorses his decade-old characterization — and the Leon Trotsky comparison is both absurdly political and somehow completely apt for Leslie
jokes.explanation: The Leon Trotsky comparison is unexpectedly specific and precise — not just 'very liberal' but 'to the left of a Russian revolutionary.' Ron's immediate 'so far, so accurate' is the perfect button. This joke works both as characterization and as a callback to the hiring scene context. The deadpan self-satisfaction in his endorsement is perfectly Ron. Strong 8 on craft.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I wanted to meet with you because I'm considering a job offer in the federal government.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: It makes me want to vomit.

jokes.text: 'If we were to work together, she would undoubtedly drive me insane, and it is possible that we would murder each other.'
jokes.setup: Leslie reads the second line of Ron's assessment
jokes.punchline: Ron predicted they'd murder each other — and the dark humor is that it wasn't entirely wrong as a characterization of their dynamic
jokes.explanation: Ron predicting mutual murder and then hiring her anyway is a classic Ron joke — his practical acceptance of difficulty is charming and funny. 'It is possible that we would murder each other' as a professional assessment is deadpan gold.

dialogue.speaker: Ron Swanson
dialogue.line: I have devoted my life to destroying government from within. It's the most rewarding work I've ever done.

jokes.text: You forgot the last sentence. / No, I didn't. I remember that part. / It says, 'Hire her.'
jokes.setup: Ron says he didn't forget the last sentence — suggesting he knows it and doesn't want to say it
jokes.punchline: The last sentence is just 'Hire her' — two words after paragraphs of negativity, which is both Ron's economy of feeling and the most touching possible punchline
jokes.explanation: The best single joke in the episode. The structure is flawless: three lines of increasingly negative assessment (absurd idealist, to the left of Trotsky, will probably drive him insane and they'll murder each other) all paid off with 'Hire her' — two words that contain an entire relationship. Ron's insistence that he 'didn't forget' that line signals its significance without being sentimental. The economy is perfect — two words carrying the weight of the episode's emotional arc. The [metallic clang] sound effect timing after Leslie reads it aloud confirms the impact. This is the kind of joke that earns a genuine '9' on craft: it's emotionally intelligent, structurally perfect, and entirely specific to these characters.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I have to say, I'm gonna take great pleasure in the systematic destruction of the government.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: That's beautiful.

jokes.text: If you just look over here for two seconds, I'll do anything. / [Leslie] I'll watch a foreign film. I'll talk to a man with a ponytail.
jokes.setup: A janitor passes outside the locked office; Ron and Leslie desperately try to attract his attention
jokes.punchline: Leslie's increasingly desperate 'anything' promises — including 'talk to a man with a ponytail' — reveal her character through comic specificity
jokes.explanation: The escalation from 'watch a foreign film' to 'talk to a man with a ponytail' is perfectly Leslie — these feel like genuine Leslie Knope sacrifices. The specificity of the ponytail detail is what makes it funny rather than generic desperation. Good character comedy.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: I moved our meetings to Thursday because I'm drunk on Wednesdays and hungover on Fridays.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: That's... that's not how that works.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Well, I'm also drunk on Thursdays, so I don't remember the meetings anyway.

jokes.text: Oh, he's gone, Ron. He's gone.
jokes.setup: Leslie and Ron have been desperately waving at a janitor through the window.
jokes.punchline: Leslie's defeated announcement — delivered as though announcing a death — that their rescuer has moved on.
jokes.explanation: Functional comedic beat. The gravity Leslie attaches to the janitor's departure is mildly funny. Workmanlike.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I made you a frame. From Ann's door.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: You made me a frame from Ann's door?

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: She didn't need it anymore.

jokes.text: After I said you were full of it, you got very angry and scrunched up your face and said, 'Excuse me, sir, but I disagree.' Did you let me have it. That was one of your top ten tirades, I'd say. You were pounding your fist and shaking. You called me a heartless thug.
jokes.setup: Ron is recounting their first interview; Leslie insists she would not have called him a heartless thug
jokes.punchline: Ron's description of her 'top ten tirades' and the detail of her 'scrunching her face' is affectionate and slightly condescending — he's catalogued her outbursts with admiration
jokes.explanation: 'Top ten tirades' is a great detail — Ron has ranked her outbursts. The specificity of 'scrunched up your face' and the fact that he admires her anger is a lovely character beat with comic value. Works as both comedy and heartfelt storytelling.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Ron, this is so sweet. You're being... sentimental.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: You're being downright tender.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: You're practically maudlin right now.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Ron Swanson, you're being positively lachrymose!

jokes.text: I would rather work with a person like that than with a milquetoast yes-man.
jokes.setup: Ron explains why he hired Leslie despite her tirade
jokes.punchline: His use of 'milquetoast' — a perfectly Ron Swanson word — makes a genuine character statement while being inherently funny
jokes.explanation: 'Milquetoast yes-man' is a phrase that could only come from Ron Swanson — the word choice is anachronistic and perfectly on-brand. The joke is mild but the characterization is strong.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Why is breakfast food reserved only for breakfast?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Because it's the most important meal of the day, Ron. You eat it, you move on with your life.

jokes.text: Yeah, I was being really optimistic. [Leslie reads: 'I promise I would never raise my voice at you if we worked together.']
jokes.setup: Leslie reads her own thank-you note promising not to raise her voice at Ron
jokes.punchline: Ron's flat 'Yeah, I was being really optimistic' — except it's Leslie who was optimistic, which he attributes to himself for believing her
jokes.explanation: The joke flips the optimism — it's Ron saying he was optimistic for believing her promise, which is a nice self-deprecating beat from him. The dry delivery and the subtext (of course she raised her voice repeatedly) makes it land. Good economy.

jokes.text: That was the real reason I hired you. Those brownies were damn good.
jokes.setup: The scene has built to the emotional explanation of why Ron hired Leslie despite their obvious incompatibility
jokes.punchline: After a genuinely touching revelation about appreciating her passion and integrity, he deflates it: the brownies were the real reason
jokes.explanation: This joke is structurally elegant — a long emotional buildup (the tirade, the passion, the integrity) deflated by food. Ron's emotional deflection via food is deeply in character and earns a laugh not just from the misdirection but from understanding that for Ron, 'damn good brownies' might actually be a higher compliment than he'd ever say directly. The joke works on two levels: as comedy and as Ron's particular form of affection. Strong 8 on craft.

jokes.text: Okay, playtime is over. I'm getting out of here once and for all.
jokes.setup: Leslie has guessed that Ron had a nervous breakdown over being 1/4 French.
jokes.punchline: Ron's response isn't denial — it's immediate, decisive action to end the conversation. His reaction to the guess is to attempt escape, which functions as a tacit acknowledgment.
jokes.explanation: The humor here is in what Ron DOESN'T say — he neither confirms nor denies, he just decides to leave. The deflection by action is funny but relies on the prior joke. Mid-tier.

jokes.text: Two years ago, you found out you were 1/4 French, and you had a nervous breakdown.
jokes.setup: Leslie is guessing wrong reasons why Ron is angry at her
jokes.punchline: That Ron had a nervous breakdown upon discovering French ancestry is a perfect piece of character mythology — entirely believable for Ron
jokes.explanation: This is a great joke precisely because it's presented as a wrong guess but is completely plausible. The idea that Ron Swanson — hyper-masculine, American exceptionalist, meat-worshipping libertarian — would have a nervous breakdown upon discovering French heritage is hilarious and character-perfect. The specificity of '1/4 French' (not half, not fully French) is the right amount. High character integration, high originality.

jokes.text: Apparently, Craig is studying yoga. These are the only dry clothes I could find.
jokes.setup: Ron got soaked by the fire sprinkler he triggered; Leslie finds replacement clothes
jokes.punchline: The replacement clothes are Craig's yoga clothes — implying Ron Swanson is now wearing stretch fabric yoga attire (an extreme violation of his dignity)
jokes.explanation: Primarily a visual joke — Ron Swanson in yoga clothes is a strong image. The setup (Craig studying yoga) pays off immediately with the physical comedy of Ron's humiliation. Good visual gag dependent on the audience imagining Nick Offerman in yoga pants.

jokes.text: Well, you look great. / I feel extremely angry.
jokes.setup: Ron is wearing Craig's yoga clothes
jokes.punchline: Ron's response to 'you look great' is the most Ron possible answer — not embarrassment, not humor, but pure stated anger
jokes.explanation: 'I feel extremely angry' is a top-tier Ron Swanson line. The joke works because the expected response to a compliment is acknowledgment or deflection; Ron's response is a completely unrelated emotional report delivered with full sincerity. The economy is perfect — four words capturing his entire psychological state. High character integration: this response is so specific to Ron that it's almost a catchphrase. Strong 8 on craft.

jokes.text: Oh, come on. Stop whining, you big baby. I've seen you with your eyebrows blown off. I've seen you without a mustache. I've seen it all.
jokes.setup: Ron is angry about being in yoga clothes
jokes.punchline: Leslie's 'I've seen it all' includes a history of Ron indignities — eyebrows blown off and mustache-less are both brilliant specific character details
jokes.explanation: The list works because both items are perfect: 'eyebrows blown off' implies a characteristic Ron Swanson accident (probably involving something dangerous), and 'without a mustache' is a known horror for Swanson fans, referencing a real episode plot point. Leslie's casual familiarity with his most vulnerable moments is both funny and touching.

jokes.text: to these 'workplace proximity associates'?
jokes.setup: Leslie is pressing Ron to open up about his feelings
jokes.punchline: She uses Ron's own phrase ('work proximity associates') back at him with air-quote sarcasm
jokes.explanation: A solid callback to one of the episode's best earlier jokes. Leslie weaponizing Ron's own coinage against him is emotionally smart and comedically effective. The implied air quotes add dimension to an already good line.

jokes.text: I didn't want her to go, as she had become one of my closest workplace acquaintances.
jokes.setup: Ron is explaining that Leslie took April away; he's admitting it hurt
jokes.punchline: He can't bring himself to say 'friend' — so April, someone he clearly loves, is elevated only to 'workplace acquaintance'
jokes.explanation: A variation on the 'work proximity associates' joke that works as a callback and on its own. Ron's inability to use the word 'friend' even when clearly describing one is both funny and slightly heartbreaking. 'Workplace acquaintances' as the ceiling of his admitted relationships — even for April — is perfect. Good craft and emotional resonance.

jokes.text: Just didn't recognize anyone. So I made a decision. An unthinkable decision.
jokes.setup: Ron is describing the moment he decided to leave Parks
jokes.punchline: 'An unthinkable decision' is played with dramatic gravity — which makes the reveal (that he started a building company) funnier by contrast
jokes.explanation: The dramatic framing for a decision that turns out to be 'start a building company' is a mild misdirection joke. It works but isn't particularly inventive — the setup is more about suspense than comedy.

jokes.text: I was gonna ask you for a job. In the federal government. Just saying it out loud feels dirty.
jokes.setup: Leslie guesses Ron was going to ask her something important at the lunch he never got
jokes.punchline: The reveal — that Ron Swanson, anti-government libertarian, was going to ask Leslie for a government job — is the episode's emotional bombshell delivered as comedy. 'Just saying it out loud feels dirty' is the perfect Ron response to his own admission.
jokes.explanation: The second-best joke in the episode and the emotional revelation that everything has been building toward. Ron Swanson — who has spent years articulating his contempt for government — admitting he wanted to join a federal agency is a perfect character comedy moment that's also genuinely moving. 'Just saying it out loud feels dirty' is a magnificent button: it maintains Ron's voice perfectly while acknowledging the enormity of the admission. The joke earns its score because it's been set up by the entire series, not just this episode. Near-perfect character integration.

jokes.text: [Morning: Ron playing saxophone, Leslie singing badly, office covered in beer bottles and balloon debris; Ben walks in] 'Well, this is different from what I expected to find.'
jokes.setup: Ben locked them in expecting a tense standoff; he returns to find them reconciled in a chaotic celebratory mess
jokes.punchline: Ben's flat understatement about finding a drunk saxophone jam session amid balloon debris is the perfect response
jokes.explanation: A great visual comedy beat. The contrast between what Ben planned (a difficult conversation) and what he finds (a chaotic celebration) is funny, and his deadpan 'this is different' is perfect Ben Wyatt energy. The visual of Ron Swanson playing saxophone in yoga clothes amid balloon confetti is comedy gold even without dialogue.

jokes.text: [Leslie and Ron, having apparently reconciled, are discovered the next morning — Ron playing saxophone, Leslie singing wrong Billy Joel lyrics, both drunk/hungover at 2 PM]
jokes.setup: Ben expected to find them either reconciled soberly or still feuding. He opens the door the next morning.
jokes.punchline: Instead he finds them drunk, Leslie singing wrong Billy Joel lyrics (the fake ones from earlier) and Ron playing saxophone — having apparently resolved everything through chaos.
jokes.explanation: A strong visual payoff to the entire episode. The callback to the fake Billy Joel lyrics — now sung joyfully as a celebration rather than as torture — completes the arc. Ron playing saxophone while Leslie sings wrong words is a perfect image of their friendship restored. Ben's understated reaction ('Well, this is different from what I expected') is the button. High rewatch bonus.

jokes.text: Morning, guys. / What did you do to the office? Ron, you're wearing my yoga clothes. You're gonna stretch out the elastic.
jokes.setup: The team enters the destroyed office
jokes.punchline: Craig's reaction prioritizes the yoga clothes elastic over the general destruction — perfectly capturing Craig's self-centered anxiety
jokes.explanation: Craig's priority system (yoga clothes elastic > general office destruction) is good character comedy. The callback to the yoga clothes works and Craig's very specific anxiety is well-deployed. The 'stretch out the elastic' concern is detailed and funny.

jokes.text: I moved our meetings to tomorrow because you are drunk and hungover simultaneously at 2:00 in the afternoon.
jokes.setup: Leslie and Ron are clearly in a state of post-celebration disarray at mid-afternoon
jokes.punchline: Ben's observation that they are 'drunk and hungover simultaneously' is a logistically accurate and hilariously specific assessment
jokes.explanation: 'Drunk and hungover simultaneously' is physiologically plausible and very funny as a descriptor. Ben's practical management of the situation (just moving meetings rather than expressing any concern) is good character comedy. The specificity of '2:00 in the afternoon' makes it better.

jokes.text: Ron, Ron, Ron, Ron, Ron. / We just spent 12 hours together, woman.
jokes.setup: Leslie immediately launches into an enthusiastic hug sequence upon seeing Ron
jokes.punchline: Ron's weary 'We just spent 12 hours together, woman' treats her excitement as vaguely irrational
jokes.explanation: 'We just spent 12 hours together, woman' is a great economy joke. Ron's weariness at Leslie's enthusiasm and his use of 'woman' as a mildly exasperated address is very on-brand. The joke encapsulates their dynamic in nine words.

jokes.text: I have three years' worth of hugs to force upon you against your will.
jokes.setup: Ron protests Leslie's immediate hugging after 12 hours together
jokes.punchline: 'Force upon you against your will' is Leslie acknowledging Ron's hug-aversion while declaring she'll do it anyway — the consent framing is funnier than a simple 'I don't care'
jokes.explanation: The joke is Leslie's honest acknowledgment that Ron doesn't want what she's about to do, and she'll do it anyway. 'Force upon you against your will' has mock-legal gravity that's perfectly Leslie. It's warm and funny simultaneously.

jokes.text: You do realize I gave you this picture six hours ago. / The frame is the gift.
jokes.setup: Ron gives Leslie a framed picture as a peace offering; the picture is one Leslie gave him
jokes.punchline: 'The frame is the gift' — Ron's completely confident statement about recycling a gift back to its original giver is both audacious and somehow perfect for him
jokes.explanation: One of the best jokes in the episode. 'The frame is the gift' is delivered with total Ron Swanson conviction — no embarrassment, no hedging. The joke works because it's technically true and completely brazen at the same time. It also lands beautifully in context: the frame is made from Ann's salvaged door, which makes the 'frame is the gift' line both a funny deflection AND the emotional truth. Perfect economy: four words that work on multiple levels. Highly quotable.

jokes.text: Ron. You big, fat, giant sap. / That seems unnecessary.
jokes.setup: Leslie is moved by the frame gift and calls Ron a sap.
jokes.punchline: Ron's objection isn't to 'sap' — it's to the 'big, fat, giant' modifiers. He finds the redundancy unnecessary rather than the characterization itself.
jokes.explanation: Beautifully calibrated joke. Ron tacitly accepts 'sap' while objecting to the excess of adjectives — his precision-mindedness and refusal to accept imprecise language overrides his dignity even in a tender moment. 'That seems unnecessary' is perfect: measured, specific, and a little wounded. Very Ron. Highly quotable.

jokes.text: But I feel bad. I don't have anything for you. I — For the first time in my life, I am present-less.
jokes.setup: Leslie loves Ron's gift and wants to reciprocate
jokes.punchline: 'Present-less' as a coinage — someone without a present — is a very Leslie word creation, delivered with genuine distress
jokes.explanation: 'Present-less' is a small but characterful joke — Leslie inventing a word for the condition of having no present to give, and treating it as a genuine life crisis. The 'for the first time in my life' escalation is a nice touch.

jokes.text: Why does anybody in the world ever eat anything but breakfast food? / People are idiots, Ron.
jokes.setup: Ron and Leslie are heading to JJ's Diner for breakfast food
jokes.punchline: Ron's philosophical question about breakfast food is answered by Leslie with flat agreement — 'People are idiots, Ron' — which validates his worldview while being absurd
jokes.explanation: The episode's final joke is a near-perfect closer. Ron's earnest philosophical question about breakfast food is absurd in its sincerity; Leslie's immediate, flat agreement ('People are idiots, Ron') is both funny and touching — it's the two of them back in sync. 'People are idiots, Ron' is an exceptionally quotable line, delivered as a complete worldview in four words. The joke works as a coda to their reconciliation and as pure comedy. One of the episode's top performers.

tmdb_overview: Leslie and Ron attempt to work out their differences.
insight: Leslie and Ron's 55-joke structure escalates character conflict into absurdist territory seamlessly.
